title: Seed, Lamp and Storm
sum: Jesus teaches the crowd from a boat in parables: a sower whose seed mostly fails and then yields a huge harvest, a lamp meant for the lampstand, seed that grows while the farmer sleeps, and a mustard seed that becomes a shelter for birds. In private he tells the Twelve and others that they have been given the mystery of God's kingdom, while to outsiders everything comes in parables, in words that echo Isaiah's commission to a people who look and do not see. He explains the sower: the message meets Satan, hardship and the worries of the age, but in good soil it bears fruit.

That evening he crosses the lake with his disciples. A violent storm fills the boat while he sleeps on the cushion in the stern. They wake him with a complaint, he silences the wind and the sea like a demon, and he asks why they are timid and still without faith. Filled with a great fear, they ask the chapter's question: Who can this be?
readings: Most scholars agree that the parables of the sower, the mustard seed and the seed growing by itself come from Jesus' own teaching about God's kingdom: small, hidden and opposed now, sure to reach a great harvest. The calming of the storm is read by believers as a miracle remembered by the disciples, and by many critical scholars as a story shaped by the Psalms' picture of God stilling the sea; both agree on what Mark wants it to say about who Jesus is.
Read as Mark's key to his Gospel

Mary Ann Tolbert and others read the sower as a map of Mark's whole story: the scribes from Jerusalem are the hard path, the disciples (and Peter, the "Rock") are the rocky ground who welcome the word and fall away under persecution, the rich man is the thorny ground, and the people who receive healing by faith are the good soil. The storm that follows at once is the first test of the rocky ground.

The chapter is soaked in Israel's Scriptures: Isaiah 6 on a people who will not hear, Daniel's and Ezekiel's great trees where the birds nest, Joel's sickle at harvest, and Jonah and Psalm 107 behind the storm. In the Psalms only the LORD rules the raging sea, so the disciples' last question already has its answer.

views.H: Galilee's farming life lies behind every parable: hand-sowing on stony hillsides, one-room houses lit by a single clay lamp, mustard as a weedy field crop. The storm fits the lake's sudden squalls, and the fishing boat found at Ginosar in 1986 shows the kind of boat that carried Jesus and the Twelve. Mark keeps small physical details, the cushion in the stern and the other boats, which Matthew and Luke drop.
views.C: Mark 4 is the source of Matthew 13 and Luke 8 on most views. Matthew drops the seed growing by itself and adds four parables; Matthew turns Mark's "so that" (4:12) into "because" (Matthew 13:13); Luke keeps "so that" but drops Mark's last clause, about turning back and being forgiven (Luke 8:10); both soften the disciples' rebuke of Jesus (4:38). Many scholars, following Jeremias, think the explanation of the sower (4:14–20) uses the early church's mission vocabulary; others defend it as Jesus' own. The storm story's wording owes much to Jonah 1 and the Psalms.
views.L: The chapter is built as a frame: a call to hear (4:3, 9), the private explanation (4:10–20), sayings on hearing (4:21–25), two more seed parables (4:26–32), and a closing summary (4:33–34). The insider-outsider line drawn in 4:11 is immediately blurred when the insiders do not understand (4:13) and then show fear instead of faith in the storm (4:40). The question "Who can this be?" (4:41) launches the next chapters, which keep asking it until 8:29.
views.J: Jewish teachers used parables (meshalim) widely, and rabbinic literature has hundreds of king and farmer parables. "Measure for measure" (4:24) is a rabbinic principle (Mishnah Sotah 1:7). Mark's version of Isaiah 6:10, ending "forgiven," agrees with the Aramaic Targum read in synagogues. Readers should take care: the outsiders of 4:11 are not "the Jews"; the crowd is Jewish, and so are the insiders.
views.T: The fathers loved the sower as a picture of preaching and of the soul's response; Jerome took the thirty-, sixty- and hundredfold as the fruit of married people, widows and virgins. The boat in the storm became the classic image of the church: Tertullian saw in it the church tossed by persecution and kept by the Lord (On Baptism 12).

deep.b:
Few sayings of Jesus trouble readers more than 4:11–12: the parables are given to outsiders "so that" they may look and not see, "in case they turn back and are forgiven." The words are a free form of Isaiah 6:9–10, where God commissions Isaiah to preach to a people whose hearing will only harden them before judgment. Four main readings are offered. (1) Judgment: as in Isaiah, God's word itself becomes judgment on those who refuse it; the parables reveal to the willing and harden the unwilling. (2) Result, not purpose: Mark's hina describes the outcome ("so that, as it turned out"), not God's intention. (3) Fulfillment: the clause is shorthand for "so that Isaiah's word would be fulfilled," which Matthew 13:14 spells out. (4) Aramaic: Joachim Jeremias argued that the last word, mēpote, renders an Aramaic word that can mean "unless," so that the saying leaves the door open: unless they turn and are forgiven.

Mark's own story points to a further answer. The secret is temporary: "nothing hidden that is not meant to be shown" (4:22). The insiders are not a closed elite; they are the people who stay to ask (4:10), and even they fail to understand (4:13; 6:52; 8:17–18). Frank Kermode's The Genesis of Secrecy argued that Mark's parables make all readers outsiders who must keep interpreting. Churches answer differently how God's hardening relates to human freedom; that question has its card at Isaiah 6.

deep.h: The sower as the plan of Mark
deep.b: Mary Ann Tolbert (Sowing the Gospel, 1989) proposed that the sower and its explanation are Mark's own key to the Gospel. Each soil matches people in the story: the path, where Satan snatches the word at once, fits the scribes and Pharisees who reject Jesus from the start (3:6, 22); the rocky ground (petrōdēs), which receives the word "right away" with joy but has no root and "trips and falls" when "hardship or persecution" comes, fits the disciples, and especially Peter, whose name means Rock (petros), and who will fall away at Jesus' arrest (14:27–31, 66–72); the thorny ground fits the rich man who goes away grieving (10:22) and Herod (6:14–29); the good soil fits people like the woman with the flow of blood and Bartimaeus, who are "saved" by faith (5:34; 10:52). Not everyone accepts the match in detail, but it helps explain why Mark gives this parable so much space and why the disciples' failure matters so much to him.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the storm as the rocky ground's first test
deep.b: If Tolbert is right that the rocky ground stands for the disciples, then Mark sets up an immediate test. The explanation says that those on rocky soil "have no root" and fall away "when hardship or persecution comes" (4:17). The very same evening the disciples are caught in a storm, and Jesus' verdict is "You still don't have faith?" (4:40). The test ends better than the parable fears: they are afraid, but they are still in the boat with him, and they ask the right question (4:41). My suggestion is that Mark placed the storm directly after the parables so that his readers in a persecuted church would read their own crisis through both: they may be rocky soil today, but the one who sleeps in the stern is still Lord of the sea. Tolbert links the disciples to the rocky ground; I have not seen the storm read as the first acted test of that soil, and the link rests only on the order of the passages and on the theme of failing faith.

echoes: Isaiah 6:9–10; Jeremiah 5:21; Ezekiel 12:2; Deuteronomy 6:4; Genesis 26:12; Daniel 4:12; Daniel 4:21; Ezekiel 17:22–24; Ezekiel 31:6; Psalm 104:12; Joel 3:13; Leviticus 25:5; Jonah 1:4–16; Psalm 44:23; Psalm 65:7; Psalm 89:9; Psalm 107:23–30; Job 38:8–11; Matthew 5:15; Matthew 7:2; Matthew 8:18–27; Matthew 10:26; Matthew 13:1–35; Luke 8:4–25; Luke 13:18–19; John 12:39–40; Acts 28:26–27

settings.to: A huge crowd on the shore of the Sea of Galilee, Jesus speaking from a boat; then in private the Twelve and others who stayed around him (4:10, 34)
settings.when: After the conflicts of chapters 2–3, when the scribes from Jerusalem have said he drives out demons by Beelzebul and his own family has tried to take him home (3:20–35)
settings.why: To announce God's kingdom in pictures that invite hearers to decide where they stand. After rejection by religious leaders and by his own family, the parables explain why the message meets failure and still promises a huge harvest, and they sort out those who come close to ask from those who stay outside.
settings.readers: Mark's church, perhaps in Rome after Nero's persecution of AD 64, had seen believers fall away under pressure and had seen the gospel's small beginnings. The chapter told them that failure was expected, that the harvest was sure, and that they must keep listening.
views: Most readers take 4:1–34 as one teaching session that Mark has arranged, with the private part (4:10–20) placed in the middle.

Many critical scholars see a collection of parables and sayings from different occasions, gathered by Mark or by an earlier source into a single discourse, with 4:10–12 and the explanation added from separate tradition.

settings.to: The crowd on the shore
settings.when: The first parable of the day, spoken from the boat
settings.why: To call hearers to listen ("Listen!" and "ears to hear") and to show what happens to God's message: much is lost to hard ground, shallow soil and thorns, yet the good soil yields far beyond the losses. Hearers are left to ask which soil they are.
settings.readers: For Mark's readers the parable explained the mixed results of their own preaching and the defections they had seen, and promised that God's harvest would still come.
views: About the sower and the harvest
Many scholars (Jeremias, Dodd) think the original point was the certainty of the harvest despite losses: confidence for disciples discouraged by opposition.
The explanation (4:14–20) and most preachers stress the soils: a call to hear rightly. Many think Jesus meant both.

settings.to: The Twelve and the others around him, privately
settings.when: When he was alone after the public teaching
settings.why: To tell those who came close that they have been given the mystery of God's kingdom, and to explain that the parables, like Isaiah's preaching, both reveal and hide, depending on whether hearers come near or stay outside. The words also warn the insiders: the same Isaiah passage will be applied to them (8:17–18). Matthew 13:13 has the same setting but turns "so that" into "because"; Luke 8:10 keeps "so that."
settings.readers: Mark's readers were themselves "insiders" who had been given the mystery. The saying explained why many of their neighbors, Jewish and Gentile, did not believe, and warned them not to become hard-hearted themselves.
views: God's word hardens those who refuse it, as in Isaiah 6.
The "so that" describes the outcome or Scripture's fulfillment, not God's wish that people not repent.

settings.to: The disciples and those around him, privately
settings.when: Right after the saying about parables, beginning with a rebuke for not understanding
settings.why: To show the disciples what keeps the message from bearing fruit, Satan, hardship and persecution, worries, wealth and cravings, so that they will recognize these dangers in their own lives and in their work as sowers (3:14).
settings.readers: The explanation reads like a description of Mark's church: some who had heard and fallen away under persecution, some choked by wealth and worries. It was a warning and an encouragement to persevere.
views: Gerhardsson, Payne and others defend the explanation as Jesus' own, fitting Jewish practice of explaining parables.
Jeremias and many critics think its vocabulary shows the church applying the parable to converts.

settings.what: Sayings on the lamp and the measure
settings.to: "Them": in Mark's arrangement still the disciples and those around him
settings.when: After the explanation of the sower
settings.why: To promise that what is now hidden in parables will come out into the open, and to urge careful listening: those who give attention will receive more understanding, those who do not will lose even what they had. In Matthew and Luke the same sayings appear in other settings (Matthew 5:15; 7:2; 10:26; 13:12; Luke 8:16–18; 11:33; 12:2).
settings.readers: Mark's readers lived in the time after the resurrection, when the secret was being proclaimed openly (9:9). The sayings told them to keep listening and to let the lamp shine.

settings.what: The parable of the seed that grows by itself
settings.to: The crowd, it seems (4:33), in Mark's arrangement
settings.when: The second public parable of the day
settings.why: To show that God's kingdom grows by God's power, unseen and on its own schedule, and that harvest, God's judgment and gathering, will surely come. Hearers are called to patience and confidence, not to forcing the kingdom.
settings.readers: For a small, pressured church this parable, found only in Mark, gave calm assurance: their task was to sow; the growth and the harvest belonged to God.
views: A warning against trying to force the kingdom, perhaps against Zealot hopes of armed revolt.
Small and invisible beginnings will surely end in harvest.

settings.what: The parable of the mustard seed
settings.to: The crowd
settings.when: The last public parable of the day
settings.why: To contrast the kingdom's tiny beginning with its great end: what looks like nothing now will become a shelter where "the birds of the sky" settle, the Old Testament's picture of the nations under a great kingdom.
settings.readers: Mark's readers, a small community of Jews and Gentiles, could see themselves in the mustard plant: unimpressive, yet already sheltering people from many nations.

settings.what: The disciples' cry, and Jesus' words to the wind, the sea and the disciples
settings.to: Jesus, asleep in the stern (the disciples' cry); then the wind and the sea; then the disciples in the boat
settings.when: That evening, crossing toward the Gentile shore, in a sudden storm
settings.why: The disciples' cry, "doesn't it matter to you that we are going down?", is a reproach as much as a plea, and Matthew 8:25 and Luke 8:24 soften it into a prayer. Jesus' rebuke to the sea shows his authority over the chaos that only God can tame. His question to the disciples, "Why are you timid? You still don't have faith?", calls them from fear to trust in the one who is with them in the boat. Luke 8:22–25 sets the storm, as Mark does, after the parables; Matthew 8:23–27 places it earlier, among the miracles after the Sermon on the Mount.
settings.readers: The boat in the storm became an image of the church under persecution. Mark's readers heard Jesus' question as addressed to them: the Lord may seem asleep, but he is in the boat.

title: Tombs, Blood and a Girl Who Wakes
sum: On the Gentile side of the lake a man with an unclean spirit lives among the tombs, unbound by any chain, shrieking and cutting himself. He bows before Jesus and, speaking for the spirits, begs not to be tormented. Their name is Legion. Jesus lets them go into a herd of about two thousand pigs, which rush into the sea. The townspeople find the man dressed and in his right mind and, afraid, ask Jesus to leave. The man wants to go with Jesus, but Jesus sends him home to tell what the Lord has done, and he proclaims Jesus through the Decapolis.

Back on the Jewish shore, Jairus, a synagogue leader, begs Jesus to come to his dying twelve-year-old daughter. On the way, a woman who has bled for twelve years and spent everything on doctors touches Jesus' cloak and is healed. Jesus stops to find her and calls her "Daughter." Then news comes that the girl has died. Jesus tells Jairus to keep believing, puts out the mourners who laugh at him, takes the girl's hand and says in Aramaic, "Talitha koum." She gets up and walks, and he tells them to give her something to eat.
readings: Read as three crossings of boundaries

Each scene crosses a line that Israel's law and custom drew around death and impurity: a Gentile among tombs and pigs, a woman with a flow of blood, a corpse. In each, it is not Jesus who becomes unclean; the uncleanness, the illness and death itself give way. Many readers take the chapter as Mark's picture of the kingdom's power over everything that separates people from God.

Most historians accept that Jesus was known as an exorcist and healer, and the Aramaic words "Talitha koum" are widely taken as a memory of his speech. The pig story has puzzled readers since antiquity, and some critical scholars see in it a folk tale or a political allegory. Believers read the chapter as eyewitness memory, perhaps Peter's, who was present in Jairus' house (5:37).
Read as a story of faith and fear

Fear and faith run through the chapter: the townspeople's fear sends Jesus away, the woman comes in fear and is called a daughter, and Jairus is told, "Stop being afraid. Just keep believing." Mark's readers are invited to see themselves in Jairus, waiting while someone else is helped first, and hearing that it is already too late.

views.H: The east shore belonged to the Decapolis, Greek cities with a Gentile majority, which explains the herd of pigs. Which town is meant is uncertain (Gerasa, Gadara or a lakeside village, perhaps Kursi). The legion of spirits bears a Roman army name. A synagogue leader was a respected local official, as inscriptions show. Jewish mourning customs, with wailing and flutes, fit the scene at Jairus' house.
views.C: Matthew 8:28–34 tells the first story with two men and far fewer details; Luke 8:26–39 keeps Mark's one man. Matthew 9:18–26 cuts the second story to a third of its length and has the girl already dead when the father comes. Mark's details (the man's chains, the doctors who made the woman worse, Jesus not knowing who touched him, the Aramaic words) are among the classic evidence that Mark was written first and that Matthew and Luke trimmed and softened it.
views.L: The chapter is a Markan "sandwich": the woman's story is set inside Jairus' story, and the two share twelve years, the word "daughter," touch, fear, faith and being "saved." The Gerasene story moves from "unclean" to "in his right mind," and the healed man, sent to announce, becomes the first missionary to the Gentiles. Fear appears again and again (5:15, 33, 36).
views.J: The chapter is full of Jewish purity law: tombs (Numbers 19), pigs (Leviticus 11), a flow of blood (Leviticus 15) and a corpse. Jewish scholars such as Amy-Jill Levine warn against reading it as Jesus breaking a harsh law: Mark never mentions the woman's impurity, and nothing in the law forbade her to be in a crowd. A synagogue leader comes to Jesus in faith, and Jesus' Aramaic command is a window onto his own speech.
views.T: The fathers saw in the Gerasene man the Gentile world freed from idols and sent to preach. The woman who touched Jesus' cloak became a model of faith that reaches Christ through humble means, and Eusebius reports a statue at Caesarea Philippi said to show her kneeling before Jesus (Church History 7.18). Jairus' daughter is read on Sundays in many churches as a sign of the resurrection.

deep.b:
Mark often starts one story, interrupts it with another, and then returns to the first (3:20–35; 6:7–30; 11:12–25; 14:1–11; 14:54–72). James Edwards argued that the middle story always interprets the outer one. Here the links are many. Both females are called "daughter" (5:23, 34, 35). The woman has suffered twelve years; the girl is twelve years old (5:25, 42). Both are "saved" (5:23, 28, 34). Both cases involve touch and both cross a boundary of uncleanness (a flow of blood, a corpse). The woman's faith comes with fear and trembling (5:33); Jairus is told to stop being afraid and keep believing (5:36).

The contrast is as telling as the likeness. Jairus is a named, respected man with a household; the woman is nameless, poor and alone. He asks openly; she touches in secret. Jesus makes the leader wait for the outcast, and the delay seems fatal, until the end of the story shows that nothing is too late for him. The woman's story teaches Jairus, and Mark's reader, what faith looks like before he hears, "Your daughter has died."

The name of the place varies in the manuscripts of all three Gospels: Gerasenes, Gadarenes and Gergesenes (see the variant at 5:1). Gerasa, the impressive ruins of modern Jerash in Jordan, lies about 55 kilometers (35 miles) southeast of the lake, too far for the story as told. Gadara (Umm Qais) is about 10 kilometers (6 miles) from the shore, and its territory may have reached the lake; some of its coins show a ship. Origen, who knew the region, preferred Gergesa, a town on the shore beside a steep slope. Many today place the event at Kursi on the east shore, where a large Byzantine monastery was excavated in the 1970s, built to mark the miracle near a steep hillside. Mark may have used a large city's name for its region, or the name of a small lakeside place may have been confused with the famous city. The uncertainty does not touch the point: Jesus is in Gentile land.

deep.title: Claude's theory: two girls, two meals
deep.b: Mark uses the word korasion, "girl," for only two people: Jairus' daughter (5:41–42) and Herodias' daughter (6:22, 28). The two stories sit a few verses apart, and I think Mark wants them read together. One girl is twelve, dead, raised by Jesus' hand, and told to be "given something to eat" (5:43). The other is alive, dances at a ruler's birthday banquet, and is "given" a prophet's head on a platter (6:28). Then Jesus gives bread to five thousand (6:41). The verb "give" (didōmi) runs through all three scenes. On my reading, Mark sets the life-giving meals of Jesus' kingdom against the death-dealing banquet of Herod's court, with a girl at the center of each. Commentators note the shared word korasion and the contrast of the two banquets in chapter 6; I have not seen the three meals read together around the two girls. It rests on word choice and placement, which could be coincidence.

echoes: Isaiah 65:3–4; Numbers 19:11–16; Leviticus 11:7; Exodus 14:28; Psalm 107:10–16; Leviticus 15:25–27; 1 Samuel 1:17; 1 Kings 17:17–24; 2 Kings 4:18–37; Daniel 12:2; Matthew 8:28–34; Matthew 9:18–26; Luke 8:26–56; Acts 9:36–42

settings.what: The spirits' plea and Jesus' command
settings.by: The man with the unclean spirit, speaking for the legion; Jesus
settings.to: Each other, on the shore near the tombs, with the herdsmen nearby
settings.when: As soon as Jesus lands on the Gentile shore after the storm
settings.why: The spirits try to bind Jesus with an exorcist's oath and bargain for their place; Jesus demands their name and drives them out. The exchange shows that the stronger one (3:27) has come into enemy territory and that no power, however many, can hold out against him.
settings.readers: Mark's readers, many of them Gentiles living in a city full of shrines and Roman soldiers, saw that Jesus' power reaches every land and every power that enslaves people.
views: Most readers take the scene as a real exorcism, showing Jesus' power over evil spirits.
Myers, Theissen and others hear in "Legion" and the drowning herd a picture of Roman occupation driven out, like Pharaoh's army in the sea.

settings.what: Jesus' commission to the healed man
settings.to: The man who had had the legion, as Jesus gets into the boat
settings.when: After the townspeople ask Jesus to leave
settings.why: To send the man home as a witness to what the Lord has done and the mercy shown him. Unlike Jesus' usual orders of silence, this command fits a Gentile land where no one would make him a political Messiah, and it makes the man the first herald to the Ten Cities.
settings.readers: For Mark's mostly Gentile church, the man was a forerunner: a Gentile freed and sent to tell his own people.

settings.to: Jesus, on the Jewish shore of the lake, with a large crowd around him
settings.when: As soon as Jesus crosses back from the Gerasene side
settings.why: A respected leader of the local synagogue falls at Jesus' feet and begs him to lay hands on his dying "little daughter" so that she may be "saved and live." The plea shows a synagogue leader turning to Jesus in need, and it starts the story that the bleeding woman will interrupt. In Matthew 9:18 the father, called only "an official," comes when the girl has already died.
settings.readers: Mark's readers, many of whom had prayed for the sick and the dying, saw that urgent, humble asking is where faith begins.

settings.to: The woman who had bled for twelve years, in front of the crowd
settings.when: After she comes forward trembling and tells him everything
settings.why: To turn a secret cure into a public restoration: he calls her "Daughter," names her faith as what saved her, and sends her off with a blessing of peace and lasting health.
settings.readers: Mark's readers learned that faith, even timid faith that reaches out in secret, is met by Jesus personally and publicly.
views: Many readers stress her return to society after years of impurity and isolation.
Jewish scholars such as Levine note that Mark does not mention impurity; the point is healing, faith and her new family tie with Jesus.

settings.to: Jairus first, then the mourners, then the dead girl
settings.when: After messengers report that the girl has died
settings.why: To hold Jairus in faith when hope is gone ("Stop being afraid. Just keep believing"), to tell the mourners that death is like sleep to him, and to raise the girl with a command in her own language.
settings.readers: For Christians who had buried loved ones, some perhaps killed for their faith, the story promised that death is not the end. Paul uses the same picture of sleep (1 Thessalonians 4:13–14).

title: Two Banquets
sum: In his hometown the people who knew Jesus as the builder and the son of Mary cannot accept his wisdom and acts of power. Their unbelief astonishes him, and he can do no act of power there beyond healing a few sick people. He then sends the Twelve out two by two with nothing but a staff and sandals, giving them authority over unclean spirits; they preach repentance, drive out demons and anoint the sick with oil.

Mark fills the time of their mission with a flashback: Herod Antipas, hearing about Jesus, fears that John the Baptizer has come back from the dead. John had condemned Herod's marriage to Herodias, and at Herod's birthday banquet her daughter's dance led to a rash oath and John's head on a platter. When the apostles return, Jesus takes them to rest in a lonely place, but a huge crowd is waiting. Like a shepherd he teaches them, then feeds five thousand men with five loaves and two fish, with twelve baskets left over. That night he comes to the struggling disciples walking on the sea, meaning to pass them by, and says, "Courage! I am." They are overwhelmed, because they had not understood about the loaves. At Gennesaret all who touch even his tassel are saved.
readings: The chapter retells Israel's wilderness story: a people like sheep without a shepherd, a crowd arranged in hundreds and fifties as under Moses, bread in the wilderness, and a path through the sea where the LORD "passes by" and says "I am." Many readers see Mark presenting Jesus as the shepherd God promised in Ezekiel 34, doing what the LORD did for Israel.
Read as two kinds of kingdom

Mark sets two banquets side by side. Herod, a "king" who is not a king, feasts with the powerful on his birthday and kills a prophet to keep face; Jesus, the true king, feeds the hungry poor in the wilderness. The mission of the Twelve, the death of John and the feeding together show what following Jesus costs and what it gives.

Historians generally accept that Jesus was rejected in Nazareth, sent out his disciples, and that John was executed by Herod Antipas, which Josephus confirms. The feeding is the only miracle in all four Gospels, and many think a remembered wilderness meal lies behind it. The walk on the sea is accepted by believers as a miracle and read by many critics as a story shaped by the Old Testament's picture of God, or as a vision.

views.H: Nazareth was a small village; a tektōn was a craftsman in wood and stone. Herod Antipas was tetrarch, not king, of Galilee and Perea (4 BC to AD 39); Josephus confirms that he executed John, at Machaerus, and that his marriage to Herodias broke the law. The denarius was a day's wage. Green grass places the feeding in spring, near Passover. Roman time divided the night into four watches, and Bethsaida and Gennesaret lie on the north and northwest shores.
views.C: Mark is the source for Matthew 13:53–14:36 and Luke 9:1–17 on most views. Matthew softens Mark at several points: "could not" becomes "did not do many" (6:5; Matthew 13:58); the disciples worship instead of having hardened hearts (6:52; Matthew 14:33). Matthew also differs on Herod: he wants John dead (Matthew 14:5), where Mark's Herod protects him (6:20). Luke omits the walking on the sea and everything from 6:45 to 8:26 ("the great omission"). The account of Herodias' first husband as "Philip" conflicts with Josephus.
views.L: The chapter contains a Markan sandwich: the mission of the Twelve (6:7–13, 30) surrounds the story of John's death (6:14–29), so that the disciples' mission is framed by a martyrdom. Herod's deadly banquet stands against Jesus' life-giving meal. The question of Jesus' identity runs on (6:2–3, 14–16, 49–50), and the disciples' incomprehension deepens (6:52), preparing for 8:14–21.
views.J: The rejection at Nazareth happens in a synagogue on the Sabbath; the mission rules echo Exodus 12:11; John's rebuke rests on Leviticus 18:16; the feeding recalls the manna, Moses' organization of the people and Elisha's loaves; the blessing over bread is the Jewish table blessing; the tassel is the tsitsit of Numbers 15. Jesus wore it, as an observant Jew. The "I am" and the "passing by" draw on Israel's language for God.
views.T: The fathers read the feeding as a sign of the Eucharist, using its words: took, blessed, broke, gave. The Twelve's anointing of the sick (6:13) is named by the Council of Trent as a hint of the sacrament of the anointing of the sick. John's beheading is kept as a feast on 29 August in East and West, a fast day in the Orthodox Church. Jesus' brothers and sisters (6:3) are at the center of the long dispute about Mary's perpetual virginity.

deep.h: John's death in Mark and in Josephus
deep.b:
Josephus, writing about AD 94, says that Herod Antipas had John, "surnamed the Baptist," put to death at the fortress of Machaerus because he feared that John's great influence over the people might lead to an uprising, and that many Jews regarded Herod's defeat by the Nabatean king Aretas, whose daughter Herod had divorced to marry Herodias, as God's punishment for killing John (Antiquities 18.109–119). Josephus also says Herodias had broken Jewish law by leaving her living husband, and that her daughter was Salome (18.136).

Mark tells a court story: John condemns the marriage, Herodias nurses a grudge, Herod both fears and protects John, and a birthday banquet, a dance and an oath bring his death. The two accounts differ in focus but can be combined: a politically dangerous prophet who also attacked the ruler's marriage. Mark's version differs from Josephus on Herodias' first husband ("Philip," 6:17) and calls Antipas "king" (6:14). Many scholars think Mark's story was shaped by popular tradition and by echoes of Esther (6:23) and of Elijah and Jezebel (6:19); others defend its basic reliability. Both agree that John died for his preaching at Herod's order.

Mark tells the feeding with Israel's story in view. The people are "like sheep that have no shepherd" (6:34), the words of Moses' prayer for a leader to follow him (Numbers 27:17), and Ezekiel 34 promises that God himself will shepherd his scattered flock and set over them one shepherd, "my servant David." The setting is a wilderness place (6:31–32, 35), like the manna's wilderness (Exodus 16). The people recline on green grass, as the psalm's shepherd makes his sheep lie down in green pastures (Psalm 23:2), and they are arranged in hundreds and fifties, as Israel was under Moses (Exodus 18:21). Elisha's feeding of a hundred men with twenty loaves (2 Kings 4:42–44) supplies the shape of the story, and twelve baskets left over recall the twelve tribes. Before he feeds them, the shepherd teaches: the first bread is his word (6:34).

Christian readers have also always heard the Last Supper in the verbs of 6:41. Mark's readers, who broke bread together each week, knew that the one who fed the crowd also fed them.

echoes: Leviticus 18:16; Leviticus 20:21; Exodus 12:11; Deuteronomy 19:15; 1 Kings 19:1–2; 1 Kings 21:1–16; Malachi 4:5; Esther 5:3; Genesis 40:20–22; Numbers 27:17; 1 Kings 22:17; Ezekiel 34:5–23; Psalm 23:1–2; Exodus 16:1–36; Exodus 18:21; 2 Kings 4:42–44; Exodus 33:19–23; Exodus 34:6; 1 Kings 19:11; Job 9:8–11; Psalm 77:19; Isaiah 43:10–16; Numbers 15:37–41; Matthew 10:1–15; Matthew 13:53–58; Matthew 14:1–36; Luke 4:16–30; Luke 9:1–17; John 6:1–21; James 5:14–15

settings.what: The hometown's questions and Jesus' proverb
settings.by: The people of Nazareth in the synagogue; Jesus
settings.to: The congregation of his hometown synagogue on the Sabbath, with his disciples present
settings.when: On his first return home after his fame had spread, after his own family had once tried to seize him (3:21)
settings.why: The townspeople's questions show familiarity closing the mind: they know his trade and his family, so they cannot accept his wisdom. Jesus answers with a proverb that places him among the prophets, rejected by their own, and explains their offense.
settings.readers: Mark's readers, some rejected by their own families for their faith (13:12–13), saw Jesus treated the same way at home.

settings.what: Instructions for the mission of the Twelve
settings.to: The Twelve, as he sends them out in pairs into the villages of Galilee
settings.when: After the rejection at Nazareth, as he begins to send them out (3:14)
settings.why: To send them as Israel left Egypt, ready and traveling light, depending wholly on God and on those who welcome them; to keep them from shopping for comfort; and to teach them a public sign for towns that refuse the message. In Matthew 10 these instructions are part of a long speech that also limits the mission to Israel (Matthew 10:5–6); Mark's short version has no such limit.
settings.readers: Wandering preachers were still part of church life when Mark wrote (compare Didache 11–13). The rules told his readers how messengers should live and how they should be received.

settings.what: Opinions about Jesus and Herod's verdict
settings.to: Each other; Herod speaking at his court
settings.when: While the Twelve are out on their mission and Jesus' name is spreading
settings.why: The popular guesses, John raised, Elijah, a prophet, show people trying to fit Jesus into known categories. Herod's verdict comes from a guilty conscience: the prophet he killed has come back to haunt him.
settings.readers: Mark's readers know the answer the crowd lacks (1:1; 8:29) and hear the irony of talk about a man "raised" before Jesus' own resurrection.

settings.to: Herod Antipas, tetrarch of Galilee and Perea
settings.when: Repeatedly, before his arrest, around AD 28–29 on most reckonings (some date it later from Josephus)
settings.why: To call a Jewish ruler to obey the law of Moses, which forbade marrying a living brother's wife (Leviticus 18:16; 20:21). John treats the ruler as bound by Israel's law like anyone else.
settings.readers: Mark's readers saw a prophet who spoke the truth to power and died for it, as Jesus would, and as some of them might (13:9).
views: Most readers take the words as a prophet's protest against an unlawful marriage.
Josephus says Herod feared John could spark a revolt. A public charge that the ruler broke God's law could do exactly that, so both pictures may be true.

settings.what: Herod's oath and the girl's request
settings.by: Herod Antipas; the daughter of Herodias, prompted by her mother
settings.to: The girl, before the officials and guests at Herod's birthday banquet; then the king
settings.when: At the birthday banquet, set by Mark apparently in Galilee, though Josephus says John was held and killed at Machaerus
settings.why: Herod's lavish oath, in the words of the Persian king to Esther, is meant to display royal generosity before his guests; it traps him. Herodias uses it to remove the prophet who condemned her marriage.
settings.readers: Mark's readers, who lived under rulers who could kill on a whim, saw what kind of power the world's kings have, and how weak it is beside a prophet's truth.

settings.to: The apostles, just back from their mission
settings.when: After they report all they had done and taught, while crowds come and go
settings.why: To care for his tired messengers by taking them away to a quiet place. The plan fails because the crowd arrives first, and rest gives way to compassion.
settings.readers: Mark's readers, busy with mission and under pressure, heard that Jesus cares for his workers' need to rest.

settings.to: The disciples, who want him to send the crowd away to buy food
settings.when: Late in the day in a wilderness place
settings.why: To make the disciples share his work: what they have is hopelessly small, but in his hands it is enough. The words prepare for their role as those who hand out the bread (6:41).
settings.readers: Mark's readers, who shared bread at the Lord's table and cared for the poor, heard their own calling: to give what they have and let him multiply it.

settings.to: The terrified disciples in the boat before dawn
settings.when: As he comes to them walking on the sea
settings.why: To end their terror by identifying himself, in words that also echo how God names himself in the Old Testament. He calls them to courage before the wind has even dropped.
settings.readers: For a church in danger, the words were the risen Lord's own word to them in every storm.
views: Some read the words as a simple self-identification.
Many read them, after the walking on the sea and the "passing by," as God's own "I am."

traditions.q: Mark names Jesus' brothers James and Joses (6:3), and at the cross a Mary who was the mother of James the younger and of Joses (15:40). Does this show that the "brothers" were sons of another Mary, and so Jesus' relatives rather than his mother's children? (The wider question of who the brothers were has its card at Matthew 12:46–50.)
views: Yes. Jerome argued from Mark 15:40 and its parallels that the James and Joses named as Jesus' brothers were sons of another Mary, so the "brothers" were close relatives and Mary remained a virgin. The Catechism makes the same point from Matthew's parallels (Catechism 500, citing Matthew 13:55; 27:56; 28:1).

The Mary of 15:40 is not the Mother of God, but the brothers are usually explained another way: they were Joseph's children from an earlier marriage, as the Protevangelium of James and Epiphanius held, so Jesus' older stepbrothers. The Orthodox honor Mary as Ever-Virgin.

Divided. Luther and the Lutheran confessions call Mary "ever virgin" (Smalcald Articles), and Luther took the brothers as relatives; many Lutherans today regard the identification with the Mary of 15:40 as uncertain and the question as open.

Mostly no. Calvin held that "brothers" can mean relatives and refused to build on the word; many Reformed scholars today take the Mary of 15:40 as a different woman whose sons happened to bear two very common names, and read Mark 6:3 as naming Mary's own sons.

No. James and Joses were common names, and Mark calls the woman of 15:40 the mother of James and Joses, not of Jesus. Most Baptists read Mark 6:3 in its plain sense: the brothers and sisters were children of Mary and Joseph born after Jesus. Tertullian took the same view in the early church.

traditions.q: The Twelve "anointed many sick people with oil and healed them" (6:13; compare James 5:14–15). Is anointing the sick a sacrament Christ instituted?
views: Yes. The Council of Trent taught that the anointing of the sick was instituted by Christ as a true sacrament, "insinuated" in Mark 6:13 and "promulgated" by James 5:14–15. It gives the grace of the Holy Spirit, strength and forgiveness, and sometimes bodily healing (Catechism 1499–1532, quoting Trent at 1511).

Holy Unction (the Euchelaion) is one of the holy mysteries, served for healing of soul and body and for forgiveness. It is given to the sick, not only to the dying, and many Orthodox receive it on Holy Wednesday.

Not a sacrament commanded by God. Melanchthon's Apology of the Augsburg Confession (article 13) calls extreme unction a rite received from the fathers that has no command of God; Lutherans may anoint the sick with prayer as a good practice.

No. Calvin argued that the anointing of Mark 6:13 and James 5 went with the miraculous gift of healing given to the apostles, which ceased, and rejected extreme unction as a sacrament (Institutes 4.19.18–21).
The Thirty-Nine Articles (25) do not count extreme unction among the sacraments of the gospel. Modern Anglican prayer books provide for anointing the sick with prayer as a rite of healing.

Anointing with oil and the prayer of faith (James 5:14–15) are practiced as part of divine healing, which Pentecostals teach is provided for in Christ's work, but it is an act of obedience, not a sacrament.
